//: Type checking for a JavaScript project (RM-002 R-07 / P2).
There are no .ts files here and there is not meant to be one. The library is
clean ESM with thorough JSDoc; this makes that JSDoc mean something. Run it
with `npm run typecheck`, which uses vue-tsc - a superset of tsc that also
checks SFC templates against their script blocks.
WHY typescript 6 AND NOT 7
TypeScript 7.0 (stable July 2026, Go-native, 8-12x faster) ships no stable
programmatic API until 7.1, so typescript-eslint and the Vue/Svelte/Astro
template checkers cannot run on it. With 29 single-file components, losing
vue-tsc is disqualifying. Revisit when 7.1 restores the API; nothing in this
file will need to change.
OPT-IN, NOT WHOLESALE
`checkJs` is false. A file joins the check by putting `// @ts-check` on its
first line - or, for an SFC, on the first line inside `<script setup>`.
Switching it on globally still reports errors in library code under a parity
freeze, which is not a review anybody can do usefully in one sitting.
THE LEDGER, AND THE RULE THAT KEEPS IT HONEST
RECOUNT, DO NOT INCREMENT. Every number below is produced by a command,
and the command is written next to it. This ledger has now been wrong
twice - A2 found it had drifted since before A1, and RM-004 B3 found it
claiming 53 SFC errors when the tree had 60 and its own itemisation summed
to 61. Both times the cause was the same: somebody edited it instead of
re-deriving it. A ledger whose parts do not add up to its total is a
comment, not a ratchet.
IT DRIFTED A FOURTH TIME ANYWAY, in the sprint immediately after the one
that wrote the rule above. RM-004 B5 added src/scripts/core/texture_formats.js
and the two counts touching it - the directory's 20 and the total 73 - both
stayed where they were. A rule in a comment asking somebody to recount is a
rule skipped by whoever is thinking about something else, which is everybody
who is adding a file.
So tests/type-coverage.test.js PARSES these numbers now and checks them.
The CHECKED counts must match the tree exactly, because an area claimed as
complete either is or is not, and the itemisation must sum to its own total -
the arithmetic A2 and B3 each found broken. The NOT YET total is asserted as
a CEILING instead: the tree may have fewer errors than recorded and never
more, so improving something cannot fail the build. That is the property B3
wanted when it deliberately left this number out of that file.
AND THE CEILING WAS PROSE. This note has said since B3 that the NOT YET
total is asserted as a ceiling. Nothing asserted it: type-coverage.test.js
checks the CHECKED block against the tree and the arithmetic of both, and
never runs the compiler. Removing @types/three took the tree 267 -> 342 and
the whole suite stayed green. `npm run ledger:check` is the mechanism now -
a ceiling, so fewer is a pass and more is a failure.
The 356 became 355 when RM-004's follow-on gave the checker vite/client, so
src/app/main.js stopped reporting TS2882 for a CSS side-effect import - the
one error standing against B3's claim that src/app is at zero.
IT DRIFTED A FIFTH TIME, in b596fd8 - the commit that added the test. That
commit wrote the paragraph above, updated the heading to 355, and left the
`1  src/app/main.js` row it had just made zero sitting in the itemisation.
Rows summing to 356 under a heading saying 355, and nothing failed, because
the test parsed CHECKED and never looked here.
RM-005 C2 removed the row and taught the test to read BOTH blocks. It also
removed a `slice(0, 7)` that isolated the CHECKED rows by counting them:
right by arithmetic accident, and wrong the moment a CHECKED area is added.
Each block is now found by its heading and read to its first blank line.
The rule that survives all five drifts: a number here is either produced by
the command written beside it, or checked by arithmetic against the rows
under it. Prose is not a mechanism, and neither is a slice index.

THREE HAD NO TYPES AT ALL UNTIL RM-005 C2, which is the thing to know before
reading any count above. three ships no .d.ts and @types/three was not
installed, so `import {Vector3} from 'three'` resolved to ANY - and with it
every three type this codebase names in JSDoc. A five-line probe was enough:
`new Vector3().notAThing` type-checked without complaint.
That made the check theatre for the half of this project that is three code,
and it hid the shape of the problem. 43 of the 355 errors were properties
'missing' from OrbitControls and PointerLockControls - the app's own thin
wrappers over three/addons - and they were missing because EXTENDING a value
of type any produces a class with no inherited members. Not one of them was a
real defect, and hand-declaring them would have written down a copy of three's
API and called it progress.
Installing @types/three took the tree DOWN 342 -> 267 for that reason, while
adding 22 errors inside the 86 files that were already at zero. Those 22 were
the price and they were worth it: nine nullable DirectionalLight uses in
lights.js, two in floor.js reachable through public API after dispose(), a
`side` parameter typed number where three narrows it to three legal values,
and an EventDispatcher with no event map, which infers every `type` argument
as never. All fixed rather than suppressed; the suppression count is still 4.
THE COUNT WENT UP TWICE ON THE WAY TO ZERO, and both rises are the point.
355 was never the real number. It was the number visible through `any`: with
three untyped and 43 JSDoc names resolving to nothing, most of this codebase
was not being checked so much as skimmed. Giving the checker real types took
the tree 342 -> 267 (three's own API, which deleted more than it added) and
then 267 -> 300 (the project's own types, which added more than they deleted,
because a Wall that is a Wall has properties worth getting wrong).
Recounted here rather than incremented, and `npm run ledger:check` is what
forced the recount - it failed at 300 against a ceiling of 267 and said so.
That is the first time in five drifts that a number in this file moved
because a mechanism made somebody move it.
WHAT B3 DID, AND WHAT IT COST
The application tier went to zero: 60 errors, and every SFC now carries the
pragma - so `npm run typecheck` fails on a regression, not just the audit
command. An area that is clean but not opted in is not protected, which is
why the pragma matters more than the count.
11 of the 71 were not type errors at all and were deleted rather than
annotated: 8 `/// <reference path="....ts">` directives in items/ pointing at
pre-migration TypeScript files that do not exist, and 3 `@see <url>` comments
whose angle brackets made the JSDoc unparseable.
Zero suppressions were added. `grep -rn "@ts-ignore\|@ts-expect-error" src`
returns 7 and all 7 are P2s deliberate ones in core/utils.js, each naming the
preserved-bug arity it pins. Seven JSDoc type ASSERTIONS were added, each with
a docblock saying why the narrowing is sound - six of them the same shape,
`event.target` to the input the component itself renders.
STRICTNESS
`strict` is on but `noImplicitAny` is off. That combination is deliberate for
annotated JS: strict null checking is where the real defects are (it is what
found the nullable-controller and the pop()-may-be-undefined cases), while
requiring an explicit type on every parameter of a 2014-era codebase would
bury those under thousands of trivia.
